notes.meaning: Five sisters from the tribe of Manasseh came forward to ask for their family's share of the promised land. Because the land was normally divided among male family heads, these women brought their case directly to the entrance of the sacred tent before Moses, Eleazar the priest, and all the tribal leaders. They showed remarkable faith by asking for property in Canaan before Israel had even crossed the Jordan River to conquer it.

The sisters explained that their father was not part of Korah's famous rebellion against the Lord, where entire families were judged and destroyed. Instead, he died a natural death in the wilderness because of his own sin, as all ordinary sinners do, leaving behind only daughters. Since he had committed no public crime that forfeited his family's property rights, they argued that his children should not be cut off.

The daughters pleaded that their father's name should not be wiped out from his clan simply because he had no sons. They asked to receive a piece of property among their uncles so their family line and memory would continue. Their request showed deep respect and honor for their late father, as well as genuine trust in God's promise to give them the land.

Moses did not guess or make up a rule on his own, but brought their legal question directly before the Lord. Even after leading the people for forty years, Moses showed great humility by waiting for God's wisdom in an unusual situation. Good leaders always seek God's direction when facing hard decisions.

The Lord confirmed that the daughters of Zelophehad were completely right in what they asked. God ordered Moses to give them a permanent land holding among their father's relatives, passing his full inheritance directly to them. This proved that God cares about the needs of individual families and honors those who trust His promises.

God turned this specific decision into a general law for the entire nation. If any Israelite man died without leaving a son, his land was to pass directly to his daughter. This protected daughters from being left without support and kept the family property in the right hands.

The Lord laid down the rest of the order of inheritance if a man had no children at all. The land would go to his brothers; if he had no brothers, to his father's brothers; and if there were no uncles, to his closest relative in the clan. This set up a permanent legal rule to ensure land always remained securely within the proper tribe and family.

The Lord instructed Moses to climb up into the Abarim mountain range to look across at the land promised to Israel. Moses was not allowed to cross over the river into Canaan, but God kindly granted him the joy of seeing it from afar. Seeing the earthly promised land pointed ahead to the heavenly rest awaiting God's faithful people.

God told Moses that after viewing the land, he would die and be gathered to his people, just as his brother Aaron had died. This sentence was given because both leaders failed to honor God's holiness before the people when they disobeyed at the waters of Meribah. Even God's most honored servants must face the earthly consequences of their mistakes.

Instead of complaining about his own approaching death, Moses prayed tenderly for the welfare of the nation. He asked the God who gives life and breath to every human being to appoint a new leader to guide Israel in war and peace. Moses did not want God's people to wander around helpless and unprotected, like sheep without a shepherd.

God answered Moses by choosing Joshua son of Nun, a man already filled with the Spirit. Moses was told to place his hands on Joshua and present him publicly before Eleazar the priest and the whole congregation to commission him. Laying hands on Joshua showed everyone that God was setting him apart with authority to take up this great task.

Moses was told to share some of his authority with Joshua right away so the people would get used to obeying their new leader. Unlike Moses, who spoke with God face to face, Joshua would seek the Lord's direction through Eleazar the high priest using the Urim. This sacred tool helped the priest learn God's decisions so Joshua and the people would know when to move and when to fight.

Moses fully obeyed the Lord's instructions by bringing Joshua before the priest and the assembled people. He placed his hands on Joshua and charged him with his new duties, showing wonderful humility by stepping aside for God's chosen successor rather than promoting his own sons. In doing this, Moses made sure Israel would have clear, God-given leadership for the days ahead.
